title: The Rise and Fall of Global Jihadism
gist: Twenty-five years after 9/11, Byman argues the United States did not win the war on terrorism but the jihadis clearly lost: al-Qaeda is devastated, jihadi terrorists have killed 122 people on U.S. soil since 2001, and the ideology failed to mobilize even amid Gaza, Assad's fall and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran — largely because of self-inflicted strategic errors, at a cost of $8 trillion and nearly a million lives.

insights.claim: Jihadi terrorists have killed 122 people inside the United States since 2001 according to New America Foundation data, a fraction of what U.S. officials feared after 9/11, when the 2001 attacks alone killed 2,977 people.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Quantifies how far realized terrorism risk has fallen below the level that justified two decades of security spending — the fiscal case for homeland-security budgets rests on prevention, not incidence.
insights.locator: According to New America Foundation data

insights.claim: Washington spent $8 trillion on its post-9/11 wars through 2021, lost more than 2,000 soldiers in Afghanistan and more than 4,000 in Iraq with over 50,000 wounded, while the Brown University Costs of War project estimates almost a million people died in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Syria and Yemen between 2001 and 2023.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
entities: Brown University Costs of War project
insights.so_what: The reference cost of a maximalist counterterror posture — a benchmark for pricing any future open-ended U.S. military commitment.
insights.locator: The Brown University Costs of War project has estimated

insights.claim: The United States may not have won the war on terrorism, but the jihadis clearly lost, because bin Laden's successors never built a durable transnational movement capable of repeatedly attacking the United States or forcing governments to bend.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline case for continued low terrorism risk premia in Western markets, insurance and aviation.
insights.quote: The United States may not have won the war on terrorism, but the jihadis clearly lost.
insights.locator: A quarter century after Osama bin Laden

themes.theme: The dog that didn't bark since 2023

insights.claim: Despite October 7, tens of thousands of Palestinian deaths in Gaza, Israeli attacks in Iraq, Lebanon, Syria and the West Bank, and the 2025-26 U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, none of these triggered a jihadi surge — unlike the 2003 Iraq invasion or the 2011 Syrian civil war.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Contradicts the standard blowback model used to price Middle East escalation risk in Western capitals — escalation no longer reliably generates transnational terrorism.

insights.claim: The former jihadis who overthrew Bashar al-Assad in 2024 quickly sought accommodation with the United States and Saudi Arabia, and the ones now sitting in Damascus seem to prefer attracting foreign investment to fighting infidel powers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: A direct signal that Syria is moving toward an investable reconstruction story rather than a jihadi haven — watch sanctions relief and Gulf capital flows.
insights.quote: the former Syrian jihadis sitting in Damascus seem to prefer attracting foreign investment to fighting infidel powers
insights.locator: The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience

insights.claim: Outside sub-Saharan Africa, jihadism no longer offers a persuasive answer to Muslim grievances or a plausible path to political transformation, even though the ideology persists — persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Separates ideological survival from mobilization capacity; the investable implication is that risk is regionally concentrated in the Sahel and Horn, not global.
insights.quote: The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience, however.
insights.locator: The persistence of an ideology is not the same as salience

insights.claim: Destroying al-Qaeda's Afghan training camps was the decisive blow, because the CIA estimated 10,000 to 20,000 volunteers passed through them in the late 1990s and without that infrastructure jihadi groups lost the ability to mount sophisticated, distant attacks like 9/11.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Identifies physical safe havens and training throughput, not ideology or finance, as the binding constraint on mass-casualty capability — the metric to monitor in Taliban Afghanistan and the Sahel.
insights.locator: Critically, al-Qaeda also had a safe haven

insights.claim: The successful model against the Islamic State used small U.S. special operations teams with local partners doing most of the fighting and dying, backed by U.S. airpower and intelligence — a fraction of the footprint of the Afghanistan and Iraq wars.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: The light-footprint template is what future U.S. counterterror commitments will look like, favoring ISR, drones and training contracts over large deployments.
insights.locator: Unlike in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq

insights.claim: The armed drone materially changed counterterrorism economics by letting the U.S. military gather more intelligence and strike faster with less collateral damage than traditional airpower.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Structural demand driver for persistent-ISR and strike-drone programs as the default instrument of low-intensity conflict.
insights.locator: The advent of the armed drone aided this effort

insights.claim: Much of the decisive counterterrorism work was mechanical and humdrum — linking a phone number here to a financial transaction there — which unraveled the global jihadi web and produced compounding, mutually reinforcing effects across training, detection and arrest.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Financial-transaction and telecom analytics, not kinetic operations, carried the load — durable demand for compliance, screening and data-fusion vendors.
insights.quote: Much of this work was mechanical and humdrum—for instance, linking a phone number here to a financial transaction there
insights.locator: Increased cooperation with allied intelligence services

insights.claim: Declaring too many enemies — the United States, India, Israel, Russia, and regimes in Egypt, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and Yemen — let jihadi groups recruit broadly but diffused their energy and guaranteed everyone would attack them, making counterterrorism one of the few causes uniting otherwise hostile governments.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: A reusable strategic model: maximalist enemy lists convert a movement's breadth into isolation — applicable to any insurgent or revisionist actor.
insights.quote: Attacking everyone everywhere all at once made it difficult to put sustained effort into achieving any single goal.

insights.claim: Jihadi killings of Muslim civilians — Saudi police in 2003-04, the slaughter of Sunni and Shiite civilians in Iraq in 2006-07 — turned Muslim publics and even previously supportive clerics against the movement, enabling governments to act with popular backing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Popular legitimacy, not force, was the decisive terrain — a lens for assessing which armed groups in the Sahel and Somalia are durable today.
insights.locator: Even more consequentially, some jihadi groups

insights.claim: Bin Laden privately warned a Yemeni jihadi leader that building a state would give the United States and others a place to concentrate their firepower — exactly what happened when the Islamic State declared its caliphate in 2014, making it both targetable and visibly brutal.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Territoriality is a liability for non-state actors facing conventional airpower — a durable rule for assessing any group that seizes and holds ground.
insights.quote: The Islamic State’s overreach in Iraq and Syria was ultimately its undoing.

insights.claim: Once the Islamic State lost territory, its recruitment collapsed because calls to defend the caliphate rang hollow and fewer would-be jihadis wanted to join a group that looked like it was losing.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Momentum, not grievance, drives extremist recruitment — a leading indicator that applies to any insurgency's manpower trajectory.

themes.theme: The remaining risk and the policy trap

insights.claim: The 2003 invasion of Iraq drove a surge in jihadi recruitment and set the groundwork for the rise of the Islamic State, making it the clearest case of U.S. policy manufacturing its own adversary.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: The historical precedent to weigh when pricing the second-order consequences of the current U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
insights.locator: The 2003 invasion of Iraq, in particular

insights.claim: Surviving jihadi groups have embedded themselves in destructive civil wars in places peripheral to U.S. interests — Mali, Somalia and Yemen — where they could convert involvement into new safe havens capable of hosting international attacks.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Concentrates residual terrorism risk geographically — relevant to Sahel and Horn of Africa country risk, shipping and mining exposure.
insights.locator: Most of them have survived by getting involved

insights.claim: Cutting aid entirely, as the Trump administration has done in many African countries, leaves weak governments and ineffective security assistance in place, which keeps jihadi groups active.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: U.S. aid withdrawal is a direct input to African security deterioration — a policy variable to track for sovereign and commodity risk in the Sahel.
insights.locator: Yet as long as the governments in these countries remain weak

insights.claim: Programs aimed at 'countering violent extremism' were not particularly effective, because people opposed to U.S. policy were disinclined to trust Washington while Muslim civilians were dying in its wars.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Messaging and soft-power counterterror spending has poor returns; budget pressure should fall there first.

insights.claim: Containment should be maintained behind the scenes — intelligence cooperation, drone strikes and training local partners — specifically to deny jihadis easy propaganda victories and limit costs to the United States.
insights.speaker: Daniel Byman
insights.so_what: Predicts continued covert, low-visibility U.S. counterterror operations rather than headline deployments — relevant to defense procurement mix.
insights.quote: All of this is best done behind the scenes, denying jihadis easy propaganda victories and limiting the cost to the United States.
insights.locator: The United States must accept that jihadism may never truly vanish
